author: ribeye
dek: Hurricane Isaias came ashore near Destin as a Category 2 on Friday, and one Dover family's fall-break beach rental is now a group chat full of roof photos.
disclaimer: Parody: the Hoffman family of Dover is fictional. Hurricane Isaias and its Florida landfall are real, as reported by the Associated Press in October 2026.
headline: Dover Family's Florida Vacation Gets Blown Away by the Season's First Hurricane

ohio_story: DOVER, Ohio — Greg and Dana Hoffman had it all planned: a fall-break week in a rented condo in Destin, Florida, a cooler full of sandwiches for the drive down I-75, and a strict family rule that nobody was allowed to say the word "hurricane" after Labor Day. Then Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the whole Atlantic season, picked Friday — their departure day — to come ashore near Destin as a Category 2 and start peeling roofs off the Panhandle.

"We watched the forecast go from 'a little rain' to 'a boathouse in Destin got flattened,'" Greg said from his couch on Wooster Avenue, where the family's packed suitcases were still lined up by the door like they were waiting for a bus that wasn't coming. "Dana kept refreshing the condo listing like the pictures were going to change. I said, 'Honey, the balcony furniture is in the next county. We're not going.'" Their daughter, who had already picked out her beach outfits and ranked them, has declared the trip "postponed, not canceled," a distinction Greg calls "a lawyer's answer from a 14-year-old."

With the storm's remnants headed for the Tennessee Valley and the mid-Atlantic by Sunday, the Hoffmans have pivoted to a Tuscarawas County staycation: Dover Park, the Warther Museum, and Friday night under the lights watching the Dover Tornadoes, rain or not. "We were going to pay Florida prices for a beach we couldn't use," Dana said. "Now we're spending the week in Dover, where the only storm surge is the line at the concession stand." Greg has already eaten the entire cooler of road-trip sandwiches. "Somebody had to," he said. "They were already made."
real_summary: Hurricane Isaias came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, near Destin, Florida, a popular Gulf Coast vacation spot, peeling off hotel and condominium rooftops and facades along the Florida Panhandle before charging north. It was the first hurricane of an unusually quiet Atlantic season and the first hurricane to hit the eastern United States since 2024. The storm weakened overnight and was downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone, but remained dangerous.

Two people were killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama, and nearly 700,000 customers were without power by midday Saturday in four states. Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a hotel in Pensacola, where the mayor said the airport "took some damage," and the storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped off part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned Saturday that the flooding risk was far from over. "The risk of flooding is still high," he said. "Sometimes these things happen a day or two days after the storm goes through. So the flooding story is not over." The National Hurricane Center said flood watches remained for parts of the southeastern United States and southern Appalachians, with parts of Georgia and the Carolinas facing up to 10 inches of rain, though totals were likely to be 3 to 6 inches, as the storm headed for the Tennessee Valley and then the mid-Atlantic on Sunday.
source_note: AP reporting carried by the Tampa Bay Times, Oct. 10, 2026: Isaias landfall near Destin as a Category 2, two deaths, nearly 700,000 without power.
